design_detail: Review article from the Netherlands Forensic Institute and the University of Groningen on post-mortem redistribution (PMR) of drugs, organized by study design: post-mortem administration to cadavers, animal experiments, repeated post-mortem sampling in human cases, ante-mortem against post-mortem comparisons, and single-time-point ratios (central/peripheral blood, liver/peripheral blood). The search is documented (PubMed and Embase, 18 April 2025, stated strings, dual screening of titles and abstracts, flow diagram): 87 publications were selected and grouped as category A (29, several post-mortem time points), B (7, ante-mortem against post-mortem) and C (51, single time point, several matrices; listed only in the online supplement), and further cross-referenced publications are used. There is no appraisal of the included studies, no extraction of their results or sizes, and the synthesis is narrative. Filed as a narrative review under the editors' checklist because it maps designs and findings without appraising them; it is not rated as a systematic review.
can_establish: Which designs have been used to study post-mortem redistribution and what each can and cannot show, and which findings the authors take as established as of April 2025: redistribution occurs for the compounds studied, starts within minutes in animals, affects cardiac blood earliest and femoral blood as well.
cannot_establish: How large post-mortem changes are for any drug or case (no magnitudes are extracted and the cited studies are not appraised), or whether the case variables it recommends predict redistribution (they rest on the authors' own studies, not presented here).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (review). Publications found in PubMed and Embase on 18 April 2025 and screened by two independent researchers; further cross-referenced and supporting publications were added without a stated method (p. 2, §2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Excluded at screening: reviews; method validation and ex vivo studies; non-toxicology; post-mortem formation or degradation of compounds; case reports and case series of fewer than five subjects; studies that measured no peripheral blood (or blood of unknown origin) and sampled only once. Only femoral blood counted as peripheral blood. Excluded after full reading: non-English language, study design, missing information, bodily material, conference abstracts (p. 2, §2), and, per Fig. 1, quality (p. 3).
sample.selection_effects: Two databases, English only, one search date. Case reports and small series were excluded at screening, yet several are cited for findings (for example in the repeated-sampling section, where 7 of the 12 references behind the 17-hour mean interval are not in Table 1 although they used its repeated-sampling design; two are titled as reports of one or two cases, refs. 76 and 77, and a third, ref. 79, as a single fatal poisoning). The 51 category C publications are not discussed individually and are listed only in the unread supplement, so it cannot be checked which of the studies cited in §§5.3–6.2 were selected. Reviews were excluded, though several are cited (Ferner, Leikin and Watson, McIntyre).

exposure.measurement: Varies across cited studies: drugs placed in cadavers after death (mostly in the stomach, also trachea or epidural space), drugs given to animals before they were killed, and drugs taken in life by the people whose bodies were studied; concentrations measured in femoral and cardiac blood, lung and liver tissue and vitreous humour at one or more post-mortem times, and in ante-mortem hospital samples.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not extracted; animal doses, routes and survival times are mentioned only as study conditions (for example, 10 days of continuous subcutaneous infusion against a single acute dose of citalopram in rats).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed, apart from one rat experiment co-administering nortriptyline with other drugs (p. 5).

comparison.controls: Within-body comparisons over post-mortem time; ante-mortem against post-mortem samples; cardiac against femoral blood (C/P ratio); liver against femoral blood (L/P ratio).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable; the review stresses that dose, route, survival time after the dose, interval from death to sampling and the condition of the body are often unknown in human cases (pp. 5–6).

outcomes.instruments: Post-mortem change in drug concentration between sampling times or against ante-mortem values; C/P and L/P ratios.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors argue that a C/P ratio marks the occurrence but not the extent of redistribution, that a ratio of 1 does not exclude it, and that an L/P ratio says nothing about redistribution in a given case (pp. 6–7).
outcomes.operationalization: Redistribution is taken as a post-mortem change in concentration (a significant change between time points, a post-mortem value differing from the ante-mortem value, or a C/P ratio different from 1), separated as far as possible from post-mortem formation and degradation, which were excluded topics.

analysis.effect_sizes: None extracted: findings of the cited studies are relayed as significant or non-significant increases or decreases without sizes, sample numbers or specimen details. The one summary figure is the interval from death to first sample in human repeated-sampling studies: mean 17 h, range 1–292 h, across 12 cited references, method of averaging not stated (p. 6). McIntyre's proposed L/P cut-offs (below 5, little or no redistribution; above 20–30, propensity for significant redistribution) are reported and criticized (p. 7).
analysis.selective_reporting: Magnitudes and sample sizes of the cited studies are not given; the category C publications are not discussed individually; the authors' own three C/P studies are summarized as supporting case-based interpretation without their results.

interpretation_gap.results_show: From a documented two-database search (87 selected publications plus cross-referenced ones), the review reports, without effect sizes or appraisal: redistribution was seen for every compound studied by post-mortem administration to cadavers; in animals, cardiac blood concentrations rose within minutes of death, with lung reservoirs and rapid acidification of blood as proposed mechanisms; in human bodies sampled more than once, femoral blood rose significantly after death for about a dozen drugs (among them fentanyl and methadone) and fell for 6-MAM, risperidone, caffeine and THC; the first post-mortem sample in these studies was often taken many hours after death (mean 17 h, range 1–292 h); ante-mortem against post-mortem comparisons carry their own biases; and C/P and L/P ratios at a single time point cannot measure how much redistribution occurred in a case.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract presents redistribution from lung reservoirs along large vessels, aided by rapid acidification of blood, as the likely explanation of early rises in cardiac blood without saying that this evidence comes mainly from rat and rabbit experiments, although the body says animal results cannot easily be extrapolated to humans (pp. 1–2). From cadaver studies the authors infer that redistribution likely occurs for all compounds wherever a gradient exists (p. 2), a generalization beyond the compounds tested. Absent changes between post-mortem samples are explained by redistribution before the first sample (p. 6), a reading the data cannot test. The variables recommended for future work (trauma, resuscitation, BMI, decomposition, body position) come from the authors' own three studies, not presented here, and the recommendation to interpret toxicology with case information despite a stated risk of cognitive bias is the authors' judgment, offered without evidence on that trade-off (p. 7).

timeline.event: Pounder and Jones call post-mortem redistribution a toxicological nightmare; Borra et al. say this still holds 35 years later (ref. 90, p. 7).
Leikin and Watson publish C/P ratios for several drugs, the data set later reanalysed by Ferner and by QSAR studies (ref. 92, p. 7).
Elliott: MDMA and MDA in ante-mortem and post-mortem samples after hospital admission, one of the 7 category B studies (Table 2, p. 4); also summarized by Milroy (2011).
Ferner finds no clear correlation between volume of distribution or lipophilicity and the C/P ratios in Leikin and Watson's data (ref. 91, p. 7).

McIntyre's review proposes the liver/peripheral blood ratio as a marker of redistribution (below 5 little, above 20–30 marked); Borra et al. judge it a marker of a drug's propensity at best (ref. 88, p. 7).

Mantinieks et al.: compilation of post-mortem to ante-mortem concentration ratios, a category B study cited for higher femoral than ante-mortem concentrations of several drugs and higher free morphine after death (Table 2, p. 4; p. 6).

The authors' own three studies (Kamphuis et al., 2021; Emaus et al., 2023; de Groot et al., 2023) relate case variables to C/P ratios of morphine, cocaine, amphetamines and benzodiazepines over ten years of forensic cases (refs. 95–97, p. 7); Tascon et al. (2023) report THC C/P ratios differing by state of decomposition (ref. 99).

replication.where_it_stands: That drug concentrations change after death, earliest and most in cardiac blood but also in femoral blood, is well documented; the size of the change for a given drug in a given body is not predictable from drug properties or from ratios at one time point, and human repeated-sampling studies are few and usually start many hours after death. Within this library, Launiainen and Ojanperä (2014) give all-cause post-mortem femoral distributions, and Ketola and Kriikku (2019, a meta-analysis of tissue-to-femoral-blood ratios for 50 drugs, per the reading list) address sampling site.

funding.funder: Not reported: no funding statement in the article.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have influenced the work (p. 7).
funding.affiliations_note: Three authors are at the Netherlands Forensic Institute (L.C.P. Borra, R. van der Hulst, I.J. Bosman), the others at University Medical Center Groningen and the University of Groningen (P.H. Elsinga, H.H. Boersma, D.J. Touw). Section 6.2 rests its list of promising case variables on the authors' own three C/P-ratio studies (refs. 95–97). Received 17 July 2025, accepted 18 October 2025, online 22 October 2025.

what_would_settle_it: The study the authors themselves describe: repeated sampling of femoral and cardiac blood and other matrices in a large series of human bodies from soon after death, with recorded interval since death, temperature, decomposition, resuscitation, trauma, BMI and body position, and with preserved ante-mortem whole-blood samples where they exist, analysed within individuals so that the size of post-mortem change can be estimated for each drug and modelled against those variables.

domains.note: Search strings, date, databases, dual screening and a flow diagram are given, but only two databases and English only, the text and figure disagree on the number excluded, a quality exclusion appears only in the figure, and many cited studies come from outside the selection.

The limitations of each design are discussed carefully, and some specific flaws are named (grouped rather than paired samples in two studies; limited reporting of sample handling), but no study is appraised individually and no sizes are reported.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Most evidence is others', but the forward-looking recommendation (which case variables matter) rests on the authors' three C/P studies, cited without their results.

Mechanisms shown mainly in animals appear in the abstract without saying so; the claim that redistribution likely occurs for all compounds and the judgment that case information is worth its bias risk are stated as conclusions.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on how much and how predictably femoral blood concentrations change after death
domains.note: Absent changes are explained by redistribution before the first sample rather than weighed as evidence of stability; studies reporting stable femoral concentrations are not summarized as such.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used. The search is better documented than in most narrative reviews, and the design-by-design reasoning is careful, but the included studies are not appraised, their results are relayed without sizes, part of the evidence comes from outside the selection, and the recommendations rest partly on the authors' own unpresented work. Citable for: the designs used to study redistribution and their limitations; the authors' summary that redistribution occurs in both cardiac and femoral blood; the list of drugs with significant post-mortem rises or falls in femoral blood (as relayed); the interval from death to first sample in human repeated-sampling studies (mean 17 h, range 1–292 h); the limits of C/P and L/P ratios; the recommended blood-sampling practice. Not citable for: the size of post-mortem change for any drug; lung-reservoir and acidification mechanisms as established in humans; case variables as validated predictors.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that post-mortem drug concentrations do not necessarily reflect concentrations at the time of death, because of post-mortem redistribution and post-mortem degradation and formation of compounds, which makes interpretation a major challenge for forensic toxicologists.

Search and selection: PubMed and Embase searched on 18 April 2025 with stated strings; 793 records screened on title and abstract by two independent researchers against stated exclusion criteria (reviews; method validation and ex vivo studies; non-toxicology; post-mortem formation or degradation; case reports and series under five subjects; single-time-point studies without peripheral blood); 104 read in full, 17 more discarded, 87 selected and grouped as category A (several post-mortem time points), B (ante-mortem against post-mortem) or C (single time point, several matrices including peripheral blood). Only femoral blood counted as peripheral blood. Cross-referenced and supporting publications were also used.
key_findings.locator: §2 Literature search and selection strategy, all paragraphs
key_findings.note: The text says 672 records were excluded at screening, which would leave 121, not 104 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Flow diagram: PubMed 524 and Embase 448 records; 793 after removing duplicates; excluded: reviews 114, method validation or ex vivo study 104, non-toxicology 219, post-mortem formation or degradation 19, case series under 5 subjects 143, no peripheral blood quantification and a single time point 90; 104 remaining; excluded for language, quality or conference abstract 17; 87 included: category A 29, B 7, C 51.
key_findings.note: Values read from the rendered figure, which is an image (not in the PDF's text layer). The figure's exclusions sum to 689, consistent with 104 remaining.

key_findings.finding: Tables 1 and 2 list the 29 category A publications (1991–2025) and the 7 category B publications (1999–2021) by year, first author and title only, mixing animal experiments (rats, rabbits, dogs, pigs) with human case studies; the 51 category C publications are listed only in the online supplement.

Studies placing drugs in cadavers show time-dependent diffusion from one high-concentration reservoir (usually the stomach) to nearby fluids and tissues, mainly the spleen and right liver lobe, with early rises in thoracic organs and cardiac blood possibly via the oesophagus or trachea after gastric reflux; human cadaver results generally agree with animal ones. Up to 48 h between administration and sampling sufficed for redistribution, which probably continues afterwards. Because every compound studied redistributed, the authors consider it likely for all compounds wherever a concentration gradient exists, with size, solubility, pKa and lipophilicity affecting direction and extent.

All reviewed animal studies showed large variability between animals; samples were often taken from different animals at each time point (small fluid volumes, especially in rodents, and repeated sampling breaches the skin and may speed decomposition), and several studies may have been underpowered.
key_findings.locator: §4, 4th paragraph (starts p. 2, continues p. 4 after the figure page)

key_findings.finding: Early redistribution in animals: morphine in rat cardiac blood was significantly above ante-mortem blood 5 minutes after death; morphine in rabbit femoral blood rose immediately after death; citalopram in rat cardiac blood rose by 15 minutes. Blood pH fell significantly within 5 minutes of death and the morphine rise correlated with the pH fall; acidification seems to matter mainly for basic drugs (basic drugs rose considerably in rat cardiac blood, acidic drugs stayed near ante-mortem values). Lung concentrations of basic drugs fell as cardiac blood concentrations rose; removing the lungs reduced, and ligating the large vessels prevented, the cardiac-blood rise; THC rose in rabbit cardiac blood at 2 h while lung THC fell.

Later changes: a longer post-mortem interval goes with decomposition and easier diffusion, and forensic cases often have longer intervals than the animal studies; time-dependent changes were larger at room temperature than at 4 °C in several animal studies; microorganisms may lower concentrations by bacterial or fungal metabolism, or raise free morphine by hydrolysing morphine-3-glucuronide (free/total morphine rose throughout 96 h in rats), an effect not seen in two human morphine studies.

Incomplete absorption or distribution at death: in animals killed soon after dosing, residual reservoirs in the gut or peritoneal cavity fed post-mortem rises. After 10 days of continuous subcutaneous citalopram in rats, cardiac blood did not change significantly at 1, 3 and 24 h after death, whereas after a single acute dose, or an extra dose 3 h before death, it tended to rise with time; in pigs killed 5 minutes after a high intravenous cocaine dose, vitreous cocaine was below femoral blood at death and significantly higher 8 h later, while femoral blood did not change significantly.

Recommended blood sampling: femoral blood from the femoral vein by targeted dissection at autopsy with a sterile syringe, preferably after clamping the vein above the draw site to prevent flux from the iliac vein; cardiac blood from the right atrium or inferior vena cava with the heart in situ; sodium fluoride tubes; storage at −20 °C with few freeze–thaw cycles. The publications reviewed often gave limited information on sample type, collection and storage.

Human bodies sampled more than once: large variability between drugs and between cases for the same drug. Significant post-mortem rises in femoral blood were reported for amisulpride, chlorpromazine, clozapine, fentanyl, fluoxetine, methadone, mirtazapine, olanzapine, promethazine, quetiapine, sertraline and zuclopenthixol; significant falls for 6-MAM, risperidone, 9-OH-risperidone, caffeine and THC. Where reported or estimated, the interval from death to the first sample averaged 17 h (range 1–292 h), so redistribution before the first sample may explain why some drugs showed no change between samples. Two studies grouped rather than paired cases across time points, which may have underestimated change.
key_findings.note: Changes are relayed without sizes; the 17-hour mean pools 12 references (7 of them not in Table 1, including case reports) by a method not stated.

key_findings.finding: Ante-mortem against post-mortem comparisons cannot separate post-mortem loss from elimination before death, nor attribute rises to redistribution when distribution was incomplete at ante-mortem sampling or drugs were given afterwards; hospital patients may differ from forensic cases (critical illness alters distribution); ante-mortem samples are often plasma or serum and need correcting for the blood/plasma ratio; tubes may lack fluoride or contain gels that absorb drugs. Femoral blood exceeded ante-mortem plasma or serum most often for antidepressants (amitriptyline, nortriptyline, imipramine, citalopram, sertraline, paroxetine, mirtazapine), and also for MDMA, MDA, atenolol, verapamil, THC, olanzapine, levetiracetam and metoclopramide; opioids varied in both directions, with significantly higher free morphine after death in two studies.

A single post-mortem time point cannot separate ante-mortem distribution from redistribution. A C/P ratio different from 1 suggests redistribution only on the assumption that cardiac and femoral blood were equal at death; because femoral blood itself changes after death, the ratio marks occurrence rather than extent, and a ratio of 1 does not exclude redistribution.

Liver/peripheral blood ratio: McIntyre's proposed model (below 5, little or no redistribution; above 20–30, a propensity for significant redistribution) is judged of limited use, because high liver concentrations mostly reflect uptake before death and a drug's volume of distribution; at best the ratio indicates a drug's propensity and gives no information on redistribution in a particular case.

The authors conclude that the “toxicological nightmare” named 35 years ago still applies: the literature shows redistribution occurs, but evidence linking it to specific variables is often absent, so practical recommendations are difficult. Drug properties explain only part of it: Ferner found no clear correlation between volume of distribution or lipophilicity and the C/P ratios in Leikin and Watson's data, and QSAR studies suggest post-mortem ionization of basic drugs plays a role.

Citing their own three studies of C/P ratios (morphine; cocaine; amphetamines and benzodiazepines; ten years of forensic case data), the authors name trauma, attempted resuscitation, BMI, grade of decomposition at autopsy and body position at discovery as promising variables, without giving results; they propose repeated sampling of several matrices in human bodies with stratification by such variables and large samples, and recommend interpreting toxicology with case information, acknowledging a risk of cognitive bias that they judge outweighed by the benefit.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says 672 records were excluded at title and abstract screening and that 104 remained (p. 2); 793 − 672 = 121. Fig. 1 (p. 3) shows exclusions of 114, 104, 219, 19, 143 and 90, summing to 689, which does leave 104.
reporting_issues.consequence: The text count is 17 short, the number later excluded at full reading; the figure is internally consistent and should be preferred.

reporting_issues.issue: Fig. 1 lists quality among the reasons for the final 17 exclusions, but the text gives language, design, missing information, bodily material and conference abstract, and describes no quality criteria.
reporting_issues.consequence: An unstated quality filter may have been applied at full-text stage.

reporting_issues.issue: Much of the evidence cited appears to lie outside the 87 selected publications: of the 12 references behind the mean interval of 17 h from death to first sample, 7 are not in Table 1 although they used its repeated-sampling design, and refs. 76 and 77 are titled as reports of one or two cases, a category excluded at screening; the rat studies central to §4.1.1 (Sawyer et al., 1988; Nagasawa et al., 2016) are not in Tables 1–2 either. The category C list is only in the supplement, so these cannot be checked against it.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's evidence base is not fully defined by its search; whether a given cited study met the criteria cannot be checked from the article.

reporting_issues.issue: The figure “mean: 17 h, range: 1 – 292 h” does not say whether it averages cases or studies, how estimated intervals were handled, or how many cases it covers.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite it as an approximate indication of how late first samples are taken in these studies, not as a precise mean.

reporting_issues.issue: Findings of the cited studies are reported only as significant or non-significant changes, without sizes, sample numbers or specimen details, and Tables 1–2 give only year, author and title.
reporting_issues.consequence: No size of post-mortem change for any drug can be taken from this review; claims need the primary studies.

reporting_issues.issue: The reference list gives the same paper twice (refs. 13 and 69, Gerostamoulos and Drummer, 2000) and has incomplete or garbled entries (refs. 35, 67, 94).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the statement that bacterial conversion of morphine was not seen in two human studies (refs. 21, 69) cites a paper also counted in Table 1 as ref. 13.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record), Forensic Science International 378 (2026) 112699, pp. 1–9 (all pages, including the reference list; Fig. 1, an image, and Tables 1–2 checked on rendered pages; pages are the article's own printed pages 1–9). The online supplement (Table 3, the 51 category C publications) was not among the files and was not read.
